channel_name: This Week in Startups · Jason Calacanis
video_title: Why quantum has been “10 years away” for 30 years | E2316
gist: Recorded at Founder University in Tokyo, Jason Calacanis interviews Kazu Nakashigi, founder of Kyoto-based neutral-atom quantum computing startup Yakumo, who argues the qubit count needed for useful quantum calculations has fallen roughly 100x (from ~1M to ~10,000) while physical qubit counts have risen from single digits to 6,000+, putting practical quantum computing on a path to around 2030, with AI already being used today to perform quantum error correction even though 'quantum for AI' remains speculative.

insights.claim: The number of qubits believed necessary to solve certain useful quantum computing problems has fallen roughly 100x over the past five years, from an estimated ~1 million qubits down to roughly 10,000, due to improved algorithms and error-correction schemes.
insights.speaker: Kazu Nakashigi, Yakumo founder
insights.so_what: A sharply lower qubit-count target materially shortens the plausible timeline to commercially useful quantum computing, which investors should factor into timing bets on quantum-adjacent startups.
insights.quote: people believing that we need 1 million cubit to solve some certain problems. But recently, that number is drastically decreased... for example 10,000 cubit... Just 1% of what we expected 10 years ago

insights.claim: Physical qubit counts have grown from roughly 1-10 qubits a decade ago to a demonstrated 6,000 physical qubits at a US university, and the founder expects the useful-qubit threshold (~10,000) and physical qubit capability to converge around 2030.
insights.speaker: Kazu Nakashigi, Yakumo founder
insights.so_what: Gives investors a concrete, named timeline (~2030) for when quantum hardware may cross the threshold into practical usefulness, useful for staging quantum-related investments.
insights.quote: recently for example, one of the United States University demonstrated uh 6,000 physical cubit... we believe that we reach to like two of them meet each others close to 2030

insights.claim: Current quantum computers are highly error-prone, making roughly one mistake per hundred to one thousand operations, which is why quantum error correction (QEC) — protecting the information a qubit holds — is treated as the central unsolved engineering problem in the field.
insights.speaker: Kazu Nakashigi, Yakumo founder
insights.so_what: Error rates, not raw qubit count alone, are the practical bottleneck to usefulness — investors evaluating quantum startups should ask specifically about QEC approach and error rates, not just qubit counts.
insights.quote: once we do quantum calculations they made a lot of error. For example, every thousand times, every hundred times they make error

insights.claim: The founder draws a direct analogy between today's error-prone, frequently-recalibrated quantum computers and 1980s classical computers that needed rebooting every couple of hours to clear memory leaks — implying quantum hardware is roughly at the classical-computing maturity level of 50-60 years ago.
insights.speaker: Kazu Nakashigi, Yakumo founder
insights.so_what: Useful framing for setting investor expectations on how far quantum hardware still has to travel operationally before reaching 'always-on' classical-computer-grade reliability.
insights.quote: probably what we expected or experienced like 60 or 50 years ago... for classical computer... we experience in the quantum computers moment

insights.claim: There are at least three competing physical qubit approaches racing for dominance: superconducting qubits (used by Google and IBM, requiring dilution refrigerators for extreme cooling), trapped-ion qubits (charged particles), and neutral-atom qubits (used by Yakumo, requiring no charge), alongside photonic and semiconductor approaches.
insights.speaker: Kazu Nakashigi, Yakumo founder
insights.so_what: The qubit-modality landscape remains unsettled (akin to early transistor-technology competition), meaning quantum hardware investors are still making a bet on modality, not just team/execution.
insights.quote: Google or IBM this kind of large amazing company try to create QPU by using super conducting cubit... some people try to use ions... and we use atoms

insights.claim: Yakumo positions itself as a systems integrator akin to Toyota in the auto industry: it does not make its own lasers or vacuum chambers, but designs, assembles, and integrates components from suppliers into a complete neutral-atom quantum computer.
insights.speaker: Kazu Nakashigi, Yakumo founder
insights.so_what: Signals Yakumo is betting on integration/systems expertise rather than vertical component manufacturing — a strategic pattern investors should recognize from other hardware industries (auto, aerospace) as it plays out in quantum.
insights.quote: our neutral atm quantum computer is something like car automotive car and we try to become the quantum computer company something like Toyota... they design everything integrate everything into one and sell a car

insights.claim: Yakumo's neutral-atom qubit approach is claimed to be roughly 100 to 1,000 times cheaper per qubit than superconducting qubits, which one industry colleague estimated cost close to $1 million per physical qubit.
insights.speaker: Kazu Nakashigi, Yakumo founder
insights.so_what: If accurate, a 100-1000x cost advantage per qubit is a major competitive differentiator versus superconducting-qubit incumbents like Google/IBM, worth diligencing further before any investment thesis.
insights.quote: one of my colleagues in Japan... he mentioned that one physical cubit cost close to 1 million USD... but we use a new drops... maybe it's it's maybe 100 times cheaper... or 10 1,000 times affordable

insights.claim: Yakumo's near-term (five-year) business model is selling full-stack quantum computers primarily to academic institutions as research tools, not for commercial use cases; only after 2030, once fault-tolerant quantum computing (FTQC) becomes viable, does it plan to sell computers in bulk/rack form to data centers.
insights.speaker: Kazu Nakashigi, Yakumo founder
insights.so_what: Gives a concrete staged go-to-market roadmap (academia now, data centers post-2030, quantum-as-a-service post-2035) that investors can use to model revenue timing for quantum hardware startups.
insights.quote: we thinking about selling our one full stack corner computers next five years, but this is not for commercial use case makers. It's only mainly for academia

insights.claim: Yakumo's founder envisions a longer-term (post-2035) business model of selling 'quantum-as-a-service' or 'quantum data/entropy as a service,' drawing an explicit analogy to Scale AI's data-labeling business model (Scale AI having been acquired by Meta).
insights.speaker: Kazu Nakashigi, Yakumo founder
insights.so_what: A speculative but investable future business-model category ('quantum data/entropy as a service') for investors tracking adjacent monetization models in the quantum stack.
insights.quote: it's time to think about how to use this corner computer as a data for example as a service... that's quantum data and quantum entropy as a service

insights.claim: Yakumo sources its high-power, high-fidelity, low-noise lasers (a critical component for neutral-atom quantum computing) from Hamamatsu Photonics and its Copenhagen-based subsidiary, forming a Japan-Denmark supply chain the founder calls crucial to the industrialization of quantum computing.
insights.speaker: Kazu Nakashigi, Yakumo founder
insights.so_what: Identifies a specific critical-component supplier and geography in the quantum supply chain — relevant to investors mapping which companies control chokepoints (e.g., high-fidelity lasers) in quantum hardware.
insights.quote: this is coming from Hamachonics in the Hamomatu Japanese company and they also have a amazing subsidiary company in Copenhagen in Denmark

insights.claim: By audience Q&A, current commercial access to quantum hardware is extremely expensive: Toshiba's SQBM costs about $90/hour to use, while renting IBM's quantum computer costs roughly $3,000/hour.
insights.speaker: audience member (Karthik, Glibzero Labs founder)
insights.so_what: Concrete current market pricing for quantum compute access, useful as a baseline for evaluating whether Yakumo's or competitors' claimed cost reductions are meaningful in dollar terms.
insights.quote: if you look at SQBM from Toshiba... it costs like $90 an hour IBM I think if you want to rent it you have to pay like $3,000 an hour

insights.claim: 'AI for quantum' is already a tangible, deployed reality: classical AI models (LLMs/transformers) are used today to estimate and correct the errors that occur during quantum calculations, forming a practical, working example of AI improving quantum computing.
insights.speaker: Kazu Nakashigi, Yakumo founder
insights.so_what: A concrete near-term investable intersection of AI and quantum computing (AI-assisted error correction) that is real today, unlike the more speculative 'quantum for AI' direction.
insights.quote: we have to estimate what kind of error happen by using classical computer... we already use a lot of AI LLM transformer for example to do quantum error correction

insights.claim: 'Quantum for AI' (using quantum computers to make AI models smarter) has no practical/tangible example yet because quantum computing power is insufficient, but the founder points to recent MIT papers as evidence the field believes a practical application is not far off — for example, using quantum-computed data (like fluid dynamics results unattainable from classical computers) to differentiate/train AI models.
insights.speaker: Kazu Nakashigi, Yakumo founder
insights.so_what: Flags 'quantum for AI' as an emerging but pre-commercial thesis worth tracking (MIT research direction), rather than an investable reality today.
insights.quote: at this moment there's no uh practical or tangible example about quantum for AI since the power of quantum computer is not enough... however uh recently the researchers coming from MIT wrote beautiful papers about how quantum for AI happens

insights.claim: The founder believes that whichever quantum computing company first achieves a practical 'quantum for AI' breakthrough will become extremely profitable, framing it as one of the biggest commercial prizes in the industry.
insights.speaker: Kazu Nakashigi, Yakumo founder
insights.so_what: Signals where the founder believes the biggest long-term monetization opportunity lies in quantum computing — a thesis investors can track against competitor announcements.
insights.quote: I believe quantum for AI once this kind of happens corner computer company makes tons of money

insights.claim: The founder expects quantum computers will never fully replace classical computers, but instead will operate as hybrid systems where some workloads route to the quantum processing unit (QPU) and others to GPUs/CPUs, with early hybrid-system demonstrations already underway in Japan (e.g., in Tsukuba).
insights.speaker: Kazu Nakashigi, Yakumo founder
insights.so_what: Sets realistic expectations for quantum computing's role (accelerator, not replacement) which should inform how investors size the addressable market for quantum hardware versus classical compute.
insights.quote: I cannot say that quantum computers take over all the position of the classical computers... but I believe corner computer could be the very very great accelerator to make classical computer even smarter

insights.claim: A recent survey of quantum researchers concluded that within the next 5-10 years quantum computers may be capable of breaking RSA cryptography, though the founder does not believe this capability is imminent within the next two years.
insights.speaker: Kazu Nakashigi, Yakumo founder
insights.so_what: A specific, sourced timeline (5-10 years) for the 'Q-Day' cryptographic break risk that should inform enterprise/government post-quantum-cryptography migration urgency.
insights.quote: one survey uh review that how uh quantum calculation researcher think about uh doors decre and they mentioned that in next 5 to 10 years we have to be very very be careful about it

insights.claim: The founder confirms a 'harvest now, decrypt later' dynamic is already occurring: some nation-states have reportedly already collected RSA-encrypted top-secret data (including from the US and Japan) and are waiting for future quantum computers to decrypt it, rather than needing to intercept data at the moment of decryption.
insights.speaker: Kazu Nakashigi, Yakumo founder
insights.so_what: Confirms an active, present-tense national-security risk (not a future hypothetical) tied to quantum progress — relevant to defense-tech and post-quantum cryptography investment theses.
insights.quote: some country already collected top secret which is already protected by RSA cryptography... they have the data, they just haven't cracked it... and once they create corner computer

insights.claim: The founder deliberately downplays cryptography as Yakumo's core value proposition, saying the company is more focused on other applications like quantum chemistry, which he says could 'create new markets' beyond the security implications.
insights.speaker: Kazu Nakashigi, Yakumo founder
insights.so_what: Suggests quantum-chemistry/drug-discovery and materials applications may be a larger commercial opportunity than cryptography-breaking for pure-play quantum hardware companies, worth weighing against more security-headline-driven quantum narratives.
insights.quote: cryptography is just one like you know very very dangerous but that's corner computer company. We thinking about some other more... quantum chemistry... which going to create new market

insights.claim: The US government has stated a goal of having a 'very useful' quantum computer by 2028, which the founder and host both characterize as an aggressive timeline; Yakumo says it proactively engages with government stakeholders on dual-use and security implications rather than waiting to be approached.
insights.speaker: Kazu Nakashigi, Yakumo founder
insights.so_what: A concrete US government quantum-readiness deadline (2028) that investors and enterprises should track for procurement/policy catalysts in the quantum sector.
insights.quote: United States listen to announce that they try to launch or they want to have uh very useful computer by 2028... it's aggressive

insights.claim: The founder identifies China, the United States, the EU, and Japan as the top countries currently making aggressive progress in quantum computing, and notes that while all countries publish some research papers, they do not share their full scientific progress with each other.
insights.speaker: Kazu Nakashigi, Yakumo founder
insights.so_what: Frames quantum computing as a strategic-competition domain (similar to semiconductors/AI) among a small set of nation-states, relevant to geopolitical-risk framing for quantum investments.
insights.quote: I think one of the top country is China, United States, uh of course EU, Japan... they of course they uh post their scientific activity by paper some of them but uh I don't think they share everything

insights.claim: Yakumo, a Kyoto University/IMS spinout, raised over $10 million including a seed round and seed extension, and budgets roughly 18 months of runway following its most recent seed extension round.
insights.speaker: Kazu Nakashigi, Yakumo founder
insights.so_what: Concrete fundraising and runway benchmarks for a hardware/deep-tech startup, useful comparables for investors sizing similar quantum or deep-tech seed rounds.
insights.quote: we expected uh for example 18 months long way after we uh we just uh completed our seed extension round

insights.claim: Yakumo's seed extension included what were the first-ever investments in Japan by two international venture firms: a US firm and a French firm (a VC specifically focused on quantum computing hardware), both introduced via a warm connection from Kyoto University's spinout/tech-transfer organization (Kyoto iCAP).
insights.speaker: Kazu Nakashigi, Yakumo founder
insights.so_what: Signals growing international VC appetite to make first-time bets on Japanese deep-tech, and shows university tech-transfer networks acting as a cross-border capital bridge — relevant for global investors scouting Japan's deep-tech scene.
insights.quote: that was to be honest that was their first investment to Japan... we also have a investment from uh the VC named Cornation... this is a top VC for uh corner computer hardware from all over... they are coming from France... that also their first investment to Japan

insights.claim: In Japan, IP developed at universities is described as a nascent 'deep tech startup' spin-out model with no standardized methodology yet; universities typically negotiate stock options (equity) or royalties in exchange for licensing IP to founders, and the founder describes these negotiations as often difficult.
insights.speaker: Kazu Nakashigi, Yakumo founder
insights.so_what: Useful context for investors evaluating Japanese university spinouts: cap tables may carry meaningful university equity/royalty stakes negotiated under an immature, inconsistent framework compared to more standardized US tech-transfer norms.
insights.quote: Japan or Japanese university have not so much experiences to use IP as a startup as a spin up... at this moment there's not very solid methodology how to use IP uh from university to startup... Tough negotiation to be honest

insights.claim: Yakumo was formed by merging two separate Kyoto-area research groups/professors (from Kyoto University and IMS) who could have started competing startups, into one combined company — a deliberate consolidation the founder frames as a key competitive advantage versus a fragmented landscape.
insights.speaker: Kazu Nakashigi, Yakumo founder
insights.so_what: An example of deep-tech founders/investors proactively preventing IP fragmentation by consolidating competing academic labs into a single company before spinout — a replicable pattern for university tech-transfer offices.
insights.quote: two professor to talk try to create independent startup similar startup but... so now you've incorporated them into the startup

insights.claim: Yakumo has grown to roughly 70 employees just 15 months after launching (April 2025), hiring 1-2 people per week, with about 50 in technical roles and 20-30% of staff non-Japanese, including two of three division heads under the CTO recruited from Sydney and Turkey.
insights.speaker: Kazu Nakashigi, Yakumo founder
insights.so_what: Concrete headcount-growth and international-hiring benchmarks for a deep-tech startup scaling in Japan, useful for comparing talent-acquisition velocity against peers in the sector.
insights.quote: the size of the company is close to 70... we just launched this company um 15 months ago... one to two hires per week
